notes.title: Social obligations in a later Tagalog account
notes.body: Juan de Plasencia's Customs of the Tagalogs (1589) describes differentiated household, leadership, land and service obligations gathered after Spanish conquest. It is later and geographically variable testimony; it does not verify the terms of Ache's hearing, an early-sixteenth-century right to the hall, or a universal rule requiring the people of Maynila to accept him.

notes.title: Channels and waterfront defenses are period-sensitive
notes.body: A Spanish expedition relation of 1570 describes a tide-sensitive approach to Maynila and waterfront defenses, but it was written almost half a century after the novel's return and from a conquest-party perspective. It cannot establish the exact two-stake channel, far-bank crossings, water depths, broken markers, or landing ownership dramatized here.

links.label: 1570 Relation of the Voyage to Luzon, Blair and Robertson volume III

notes.title: The conditional settlement is invented
notes.body: The keeper's wage dispute, Amaya's household witnesses, Dala's family's damaged work, the two channel stakes, the contested far-bank passage and Ache's conditional public duties are fictional. The ending grants Ache a place to answer for claims, not ownership of the workers' rooms or stores, exclusive command of the river, or acceptance by every household. Harun's refusal to carry a separate upriver message does not prove that Amaya reached, or failed to reach, the carrier she had mentioned for Ache's mother; her earlier offer had no stated deadline.
